extracted.intended_audience: novelists and aspiring authors preparing opening pages for agents and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting (or revising) the first ten pages of a novel so they hook readers and literary agents—what to include, what to cut, and common opening-page mistakes to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook the reader in the first ten pages
rubrics_metrics.description: You must grab your reader’s attention in those first ten pages, or they'll move on to something else and never give your book a second thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First ten pages often mean the difference between a book an agent/publisher decides to pursue and one they reject. Use this real estate to compel reading—if you fail to hook the reader here, they likely won't continue. Aim for immediate action, tension, or curiosity grounded in clarity about who/where/what.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotlighting inconsequential characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ten pages of your manuscript should focus on your protagonist; don't over-inflate minor characters who aren't consequential to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anytime you introduce a character in the first ten pages, ask: Is this character essential to the protagonist's journey? Will they appear again in a meaningful way? Do they contribute to the plot conflict? If the answer is no to all, don't spend much time on them and you probably don't need to name them. Naming signals importance; avoid creating improper expectations or crowding the narrative with apparent 'main' characters who never matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivering too much backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer authors often dump excessive backstory early on; readers won't care about a character's past until they're invested in the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat backstory as seasoning—not the meal itself. Sprinkle only what the reader needs to follow the current scene. If you're writing pages of flashbacks or long personal history, ask: What compelling backstory does the reader actually need right now? If it's not essential, save it for later. (Example referenced: Breaking Bad—start with immediate action that makes us want to know more.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burying the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Many openings spend too much time on setting/exposition or routine so the protagonist 'doesn't actually do anything' and the pace feels slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid warm-up-lap openings. The opening scene should show your protagonist discovering something consequential, navigating a conflict, or working toward a goal. Revisit mundane routine openings (e.g., full morning routines) and consider starting when something meaningful begins to happen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting with a lengthy prologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting the novel with a lengthy prologue—meaning more than ten pages—is risky and often does more harm than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the story truly calls for a prologue. Bad uses: dumping world-building or historical background; presenting a cryptic scene readers can't understand. Effective prologues are short and either tease an event that comes later (often the climax) or provide crucial earlier context. Keep prologues short and, if querying agents who request 'first ten pages,' don't waste that sample on a full prologue that doesn't show the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing the reader in the opening pages frustrates them; obfuscation rarely creates productive suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In openings we need three things clearly signaled: Who the protagonist is; Where we are; What’s going on. Give enough baseline information for readers to orient themselves—suspense arises from giving enough to make readers eager to learn more, not from withholding essential facts. (Example referenced: The Martian—clear who, where, and what immediately.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Not introducing enough conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Without conflict you have scenes that don't add up to a story; conflict should appear in the very first pages to shape the narrative and create emotional investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show tension or obstacles early. Ask: What does my protagonist want above all else—and what is stopping them from getting it? If the protagonist lacks desire or obstacles, the opening lacks conflict. Conflict can be subtle (intimate tensions) or large-scale; size matters less than the presence of stakes and friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgetting the setting
rubrics_metrics.description: White-room syndrome—an opening with no sense of place—prevents immersion because readers can't visualize where characters are or when it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground scenes with enough setting detail to orient readers without long descriptive dumps. Weave setting into action; indicate at least roughly where (geographically) and when (time period) the novel is set. Small sensory details and atmosphere can create immersion without slowing pace. (Example referenced: The Night Circus for strong setting work.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglecting the stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakes are what make a reader care; conflict without stakes won't emotionally invest readers in outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What’s at stake for my protagonist in the opening scene? If the answer is 'nothing really,' raise the stakes. Stakes needn't be life-or-death—small consequences can matter if they affect something meaningful to the protagonist (e.g., missing a bus could cost an important job interview). Clarify why the scene's events matter to the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening in the wrong place entirely
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers start the novel too early—before the story actually begins—so the narrative doesn't pick up until far later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the novel on the day the protagonist's life changes (the inciting incident) or at least lead immediately toward it. If the story doesn't pick up until 50–100 pages in, cut those pages or open at the scene where the journey begins. Most effective openings are often deeper in the manuscript than the author first assumes (examples: The Hunger Games begins at the reaping; The Martian begins with the protagonist already in crisis).
